## Statement

Let \(V\) be an \(n\)-dimensional real vector space, and let
\[
1\le r,s<\frac n2.
\]
For \(0\ne v\in V\), write
\[
\operatorname{St}_k(v):=v\wedge \bigwedge^{k-1}V\subseteq \bigwedge^kV.
\]

### Theorem

Suppose \(U\subseteq\bigwedge^rV\) and \(W\subseteq\bigwedge^sV\) satisfy
\[
u\wedge w=0\qquad\text{for all }u\in U,\ w\in W,
\]
and
\[
\dim U\,\dim W
=
\binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n-1}{s-1}.
\]
Then there is a nonzero \(v\in V\) such that
\[
U=\operatorname{St}_r(v),
\qquad
W=\operatorname{St}_s(v).
\]

Conversely, every such pair is mutually annihilating and attains equality.

The proof has three ingredients.

---

## 1. Equality for cross-intersecting set families

A pair
\[
\mathcal A\subseteq\binom{[n]}r,\qquad
\mathcal B\subseteq\binom{[n]}s
\]
is cross-intersecting if \(A\cap B\ne\varnothing\) for every \(A\in\mathcal A\), \(B\in\mathcal B\).

We shall use the already-established product inequality
\[
|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|
\le
\binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n-1}{s-1}
\tag{1}
\]
whenever \(r,s\le n/2\). This is also an immediate special case of the inequality part of Scott–Wilmer Theorem 2.4, by taking the coordinate monomial spans of \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\).

We need its strict equality case.

### Lemma 1

If \(r,s<n/2\), \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) are cross-intersecting, and equality holds in (1), then there is \(c\in[n]\) such that
\[
\mathcal A=\{A\in\tbinom{[n]}r:c\in A\},
\qquad
\mathcal B=\{B\in\tbinom{[n]}s:c\in B\}.
\tag{2}
\]

### Proof

We give the equality argument because it will later be important that the original, unshifted families are stars.

#### The case \(r=1\) or \(s=1\)

Suppose \(r=1\), and identify \(\mathcal A\) with a set \(P\subseteq[n]\), of size \(a\). Every member of \(\mathcal B\) must contain \(P\), so
\[
|\mathcal B|\le \binom{n-a}{s-a},
\]
with the right side understood as zero when \(a>s\).

If \(2\le a\le s\), then, since \(n>2s\),
\[
\frac{\binom{n-1}{s-1}}{\binom{n-a}{s-a}}
=
\prod_{j=1}^{a-1}
\frac{n-a+j}{s-a+j}
>
2^{a-1}\ge a.
\]
Thus
\[
a|\mathcal B|<\binom{n-1}{s-1}.
\]
Equality is therefore possible only when \(a=1\), in which case \(\mathcal B\) must be the full star through the unique point of \(P\). The case \(s=1\) is symmetric.

Hence assume \(r,s\ge2\).

#### Compressions

For \(i<j\), apply the usual \((i,j)\)-compression simultaneously to both families. Namely, a set \(F\) containing \(j\) but not \(i\) is replaced by
\[
F-j+i
\]
provided this replacement is not already in the family.

Simultaneous compression preserves cross-intersection. Indeed, suppose two compressed sets are disjoint. They cannot both be newly created, since both would contain \(i\). If exactly one, say \(A'\), is newly created from \(A=A'-i+j\), then the other compressed set \(B'\) is an original member. Cross-intersection of \(A\) and \(B'\) forces \(j\in B'\). Since \(B'\) survived compression and \(i\notin B'\), the set \(B'-j+i\) was already in the original second family. But it is disjoint from \(A\), a contradiction.

Repeated compression therefore produces shifted cross-intersecting families of the same sizes.

#### Shifted extremizers

We prove by induction on \(n\) that a shifted extremal pair is a common star.

For a shifted family \(\mathcal A\), define its sections on \([n-1]\):
\[
\mathcal A_0=\{A\in\mathcal A:n\notin A\},
\qquad
\mathcal A_1=\{A\setminus\{n\}:n\in A\}.
\]
Define \(\mathcal B_0,\mathcal B_1\) similarly.

All four pairs \((\mathcal A_i,\mathcal B_j)\) are cross-intersecting. This is immediate unless \(i=j=1\). For that remaining pair, suppose
\[
X\in\mathcal A_1,\qquad Y\in\mathcal B_1,\qquad X\cap Y=\varnothing.
\]
Since \(r+s<n\), choose
\[
t\in[n-1]\setminus(X\cup Y).
\]
Shiftedness of \(\mathcal A\) implies \(X\cup\{t\}\in\mathcal A\), but this set is disjoint from \(Y\cup\{n\}\in\mathcal B\), a contradiction.

Put
\[
R_0=\binom{n-2}{r-1},\quad R_1=\binom{n-2}{r-2},
\]
and similarly
\[
S_0=\binom{n-2}{s-1},\quad S_1=\binom{n-2}{s-2}.
\]
Since \(r,s<n/2\), all four section pairs satisfy the hypotheses of the product bound on the \((n-1)\)-element ground set. Therefore
\[
|\mathcal A_i||\mathcal B_j|\le R_iS_j
\qquad(i,j\in\{0,1\}).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|
&=\sum_{i,j}|\mathcal A_i||\mathcal B_j|\\
&\le \sum_{i,j}R_iS_j\\
&=(R_0+R_1)(S_0+S_1)\\
&=\binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n-1}{s-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If equality holds, all four section inequalities are equalities. In particular,
\[
|\mathcal A_1||\mathcal B_1|=R_1S_1.
\]
The parameters \(r-1,s-1\) are strictly less than \((n-1)/2\), so induction gives a common point \(c\in[n-1]\) such that \(\mathcal A_1\) and \(\mathcal B_1\) are the full stars through \(c\).

It follows that
\[
|\mathcal A_1|=R_1,\qquad |\mathcal B_1|=S_1.
\]
The other equality relations then give
\[
|\mathcal A_0|=R_0,\qquad |\mathcal B_0|=S_0.
\]

Every member of \(\mathcal A_0\) must contain \(c\). Indeed, if \(A\in\mathcal A_0\) omitted \(c\), there are enough elements outside \(A\cup\{c\}\) to choose an \((s-1)\)-set containing \(c\) and disjoint from \(A\), contradicting cross-intersection with \(\mathcal B_1\). Thus \(\mathcal A_0\) is contained in the \(c\)-star, and its size \(R_0\) shows it is the full \(c\)-star. Similarly, \(\mathcal B_0\) is the full \(c\)-star.

Hence \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) are both full stars through \(c\). Since they are shifted, necessarily \(c=1\).

#### Undoing the compressions

It remains to show that an uncompressed preimage of a common star is again a common star.

Suppose an \((i,j)\)-compression sends \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B\) to full stars through a common point \(c\).

If \(c\notin\{i,j\}\), membership in every compression pair is forced, so the original families were already the \(c\)-stars. The case \(c=j\) is impossible, since a compressed family cannot contain \(X\cup\{j\}\) while omitting \(X\cup\{i\}\).

It remains that \(c=i\). For every
\[
X\in\binom{[n]\setminus\{i,j\}}{r-1},
\]
the original family \(\mathcal A\) contains exactly one of
\[
X\cup\{i\},\qquad X\cup\{j\}.
\]
Label \(X\) by the selected point \(i\) or \(j\). Do the same for every
\[
Y\in\binom{[n]\setminus\{i,j\}}{s-1}
\]
using \(\mathcal B\).

If \(X\cap Y=\varnothing\), their labels must agree; otherwise the corresponding selected sets are disjoint. The bipartite disjointness graph between the \((r-1)\)- and \((s-1)\)-subsets of an \((n-2)\)-element set is connected because
\[
(r-1)+(s-1)<n-2.
\]
Thus all labels are equal. Therefore the two original families were either both \(i\)-stars or both \(j\)-stars.

Undoing all compressions proves (2). ∎

---

## 2. Initial supports

Fix a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_n\) of \(V\), and give \(e_i\) weight \(2^i\). For
\[
I\subseteq[n],\qquad e_I=\bigwedge_{i\in I}e_i,
\]
put
\[
\mathrm{wt}(I)=\sum_{i\in I}2^i.
\]
All subset weights are distinct.

For a nonzero homogeneous exterior form
\[
u=\sum_I u_Ie_I,
\]
let \(\operatorname{in}(u)\) be the support \(I\) of its largest-weight nonzero monomial. For a subspace \(U\), let
\[
\operatorname{In}(U)=
\{\operatorname{in}(u):0\ne u\in U\}.
\]

Gaussian elimination, with monomials ordered by weight, gives
\[
|\operatorname{In}(U)|=\dim U.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, these are precisely the pivot positions of a row-echelon basis.

### Lemma 2

If \(U\wedge W=0\), then \(\operatorname{In}(U)\) and \(\operatorname{In}(W)\) are cross-intersecting.

### Proof

Suppose \(I=\operatorname{in}(u)\) and \(J=\operatorname{in}(w)\) were disjoint. Then \(e_I\wedge e_J\ne0\).

Any nonzero product term \(e_K\wedge e_L\) has
\[
\mathrm{wt}(K)+\mathrm{wt}(L)
\le
\mathrm{wt}(I)+\mathrm{wt}(J),
\]
with equality only for \(K=I,L=J\). Therefore the coefficient of \(e_{I\cup J}\) in \(u\wedge w\) cannot cancel, and \(u\wedge w\ne0\), a contradiction. ∎

Combining Lemmas 1 and 2 with (3), an extremal pair \(U,W\) has a basis index \(t\) such that
\[
\operatorname{In}(U)=\{I\in\tbinom{[n]}r:t\in I\},
\qquad
\operatorname{In}(W)=\{J\in\tbinom{[n]}s:t\in J\}.
\tag{4}
\]
In particular,
\[
\dim U=\binom{n-1}{r-1},\qquad
\dim W=\binom{n-1}{s-1}.
\]

---

## 3. A rigidity lemma for the graph maps

We use the following elementary exterior-algebra fact.

### Lemma 3

Let \(H\) have dimension \(m\), and let \(p,q\ge0\) satisfy
\[
p+q+2\le m.
\]
Suppose
\[
A:\bigwedge^pH\longrightarrow\bigwedge^{p+1}H,
\qquad
B:\bigwedge^qH\longrightarrow\bigwedge^{q+1}H
\]
are linear maps satisfying
\[
A(x)\wedge y=(-1)^p x\wedge B(y)
\tag{5}
\]
for all \(x\in\bigwedge^pH\), \(y\in\bigwedge^qH\). Then there is \(h\in H\) such that
\[
A(x)=h\wedge x,\qquad B(y)=h\wedge y.
\tag{6}
\]

### Proof

The cases \(p=0\) and \(q=0\) are immediate. For example, if \(p=0\), then
\[
B(y)=A(1)\wedge y.
\]

Assume \(p,q\ge1\).

We use the basic nondegeneracy fact that if \(K\) has dimension \(d\), \(a+b\le d\), and
\[
\alpha\wedge\bigwedge^bK=0
\]
for \(\alpha\in\bigwedge^aK\), then \(\alpha=0\). This follows from the perfect top-degree exterior pairing.

Let
\[
x=x_1\wedge\cdots\wedge x_p
\]
be decomposable. Fix \(i\), and pass to \(H/\langle x_i\rangle\). The right side of (5) vanishes in this quotient. Hence the image \(\overline{A(x)}\) satisfies
\[
\overline{A(x)}\wedge\bigwedge^q(H/\langle x_i\rangle)=0.
\]
Since
\[
(p+1)+q\le m-1,
\]
nondegeneracy gives \(\overline{A(x)}=0\). Therefore \(A(x)\) is divisible by \(x_i\). This holds for every \(i\), so
\[
A(x)\in H\wedge x.
\tag{7}
\]

We now use the following local-to-global observation:

> If \(T:\bigwedge^pH\to\bigwedge^{p+1}H\) is linear and
> \(T(x)\in H\wedge x\) for every decomposable \(x\), then
> \(T(x)=h\wedge x\) for a fixed \(h\in H\).

To verify it, choose a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_m\). For every \(p\)-subset \(I\), write
\[
T(e_I)=h_I\wedge e_I,
\]
where \(h_I\) is determined modulo \(\langle e_i:i\in I\rangle\). If \(a\notin I\), let \(c_{I,a}\) be the coefficient of \(e_a\) in \(h_I\).

Suppose \(I=K\cup\{i\}\) and \(I'=K\cup\{j\}\) are adjacent \(p\)-sets, neither containing \(a\). Since
\[
e_K\wedge(e_i+e_j)
\]
is decomposable, applying the divisibility condition to its image and then quotienting by
\[
\langle e_k:k\in K\rangle+\langle e_i+e_j\rangle
\]
shows, by comparing the \(e_a\wedge e_i\) coefficient, that
\[
c_{I,a}=c_{I',a}.
\]
The graph of \(p\)-subsets avoiding \(a\), adjacent when they differ in one element, is connected. Hence \(c_{I,a}\) depends only on \(a\); call it \(c_a\). Setting
\[
h=\sum_ac_ae_a
\]
gives \(T(e_I)=h\wedge e_I\) for every \(I\), and hence \(T=L_h\).

Applying this observation to (7), there is \(h\in H\) with
\[
A(x)=h\wedge x.
\]
Substitution into (5) gives
\[
x\wedge\bigl(B(y)-h\wedge y\bigr)=0
\]
for all \(x\in\bigwedge^pH\). Since
\[
p+(q+1)\le m,
\]
nondegeneracy once again implies
\[
B(y)=h\wedge y.
\]
This proves (6). ∎

---

## 4. Proof of the theorem

Choose the basis and initial supports used above. By (4), there is a common index \(t\). Put
\[
e=e_t,\qquad
H=\operatorname{span}\{e_i:i\ne t\}.
\]
Thus
\[
V=\langle e\rangle\oplus H.
\]

The projection
\[
\pi_r:\bigwedge^rV\longrightarrow e\wedge\bigwedge^{r-1}H
\]
is injective on \(U\). Indeed, a nonzero element of its kernel would have every monomial support avoiding \(t\), contradicting (4). Since both \(U\) and the target have dimension \(\binom{n-1}{r-1}\), this restriction is an isomorphism.

Consequently, with \(p=r-1\), there is a linear map
\[
A:\bigwedge^pH\longrightarrow\bigwedge^{p+1}H
\]
such that
\[
U=\{e\wedge x+A(x):x\in\bigwedge^pH\}.
\tag{8}
\]
Likewise, with \(q=s-1\), there is
\[
B:\bigwedge^qH\longrightarrow\bigwedge^{q+1}H
\]
such that
\[
W=\{e\wedge y+B(y):y\in\bigwedge^qH\}.
\tag{9}
\]

For arbitrary \(x,y\), mutual annihilation gives
\[
0=(e\wedge x+A(x))\wedge(e\wedge y+B(y)).
\]
Taking the component containing \(e\) yields
\[
x\wedge B(y)+(-1)^{p+1}A(x)\wedge y=0,
\]
or equivalently
\[
A(x)\wedge y=(-1)^p x\wedge B(y).
\tag{10}
\]

Now
\[
\dim H=n-1
\]
and
\[
p+q+2=r+s\le n-1,
\]
because \(r,s<n/2\). Lemma 3 therefore applies. There is \(h\in H\) such that
\[
A(x)=h\wedge x,\qquad B(y)=h\wedge y.
\]

Set
\[
v=e+h.
\]
Equations (8) and (9) become
\[
U=\{v\wedge x:x\in\bigwedge^{r-1}H\},
\qquad
W=\{v\wedge y:y\in\bigwedge^{s-1}H\}.
\]
Since \(v\notin H\), one has \(V=\langle v\rangle\oplus H\), and hence
\[
v\wedge\bigwedge^{r-1}H
=
v\wedge\bigwedge^{r-1}V,
\]
with the analogous identity in degree \(s\). Therefore
\[
U=v\wedge\bigwedge^{r-1}V,
\qquad
W=v\wedge\bigwedge^{s-1}V.
\]

Conversely, such spaces are mutually annihilating because every cross-product contains \(v\wedge v=0\), and their dimensions are
\[
\binom{n-1}{r-1},\qquad
\binom{n-1}{s-1}.
\]

This completes the characterization.

## Gaps and scope

There is no remaining mathematical gap under the stated strict hypotheses. The proof uses only the already-proved product inequality from Theorem 2.4. It does not characterize boundary cases with \(r=n/2\) or \(s=n/2\), where both the set-family equality analysis and the rigidity argument can acquire additional possibilities. I have not independently checked whether this short argument already appears in later literature.
